title: The five beloved
hookLine: Daya Ram, Dharam Das, Himmat Rai, Mohkam Chand and Sahib Chand step forward, from different castes and regions

cards: The crowd on the hillside has thinned. Some have run. The ones who stayed are staring at the tent, where five men went in and none came out.
Then the flap opens. Out walks the Guru, and behind him, all five. Alive.
Dressed alike, tradition says, in fresh saffron-colored clothes and turbans, each carrying a sword, standing tall beside him. A moment ago the crowd was terrified.
Now it's looking at five ordinary men who have become something new. The Guru calls them the Panj Pyare.

teach.b: Panj means five, pyare means beloved: the five beloved ones. Now look at who they were, because this is the point.
Daya Ram was a shopkeeper from Lahore, in the west. Dharam Das, a farmer from near Delhi. Himmat Rai, a water-carrier from Puri, on the eastern coast.
Mohkam Chand, a washerman, or by some accounts a cloth printer, from Dwarka, far away on the western sea. Sahib Chand, a barber from Bidar, in the south.
In the society around them, most of these men would never have eaten at the same table. Their castes ranked them high and low. Their homes spanned the subcontinent.
And the Guru put them side by side, dressed alike, as one. Then the lovely detail Sikhs point to: their names. Daya means compassion.
Dharam, righteousness, doing what's right. Himmat, courage. Mohkam, steadfastness, firmness.
And Sahib, sovereignty, a kind of noble dignity.
Five names that make a portrait, and Sikhs often say that's what the Khalsa is meant to be.
After that day they took new names ending in Singh, and they're remembered as Bhai Daya Singh, Bhai Dharam Singh, Bhai Himmat Singh, Bhai Mohkam Singh and Bhai Sahib Singh. And they're still present.

teach.h: FIVE STILL STAND IN THEIR PLACE.
teach.b: At every Sikh initiation, and at the head of processions, five Sikhs stand in their place as the Panj Pyare.
Five beloved, from everywhere, for everyone.

how: At every amrit initiation, five initiated Sikhs serve as the Panj Pyare, and five Sikhs in their place lead nagar kirtan processions at Vaisakhi and other festivals.

o: the five beloved who answered the Guru's call
the five rivers that give Punjab its name
the first five Gurus of the Sikh line

games.q: what the names mean — tap the pairs.

s: the five all came from the same caste and town
they came from Lahore, near Delhi, Puri, Dwarka and Bidar, and from different castes.
their names mean compassion, righteousness, courage, steadfastness and dignity
Sikhs often say the names make a portrait of the Khalsa.
the Panj Pyare exist only in history now
at every initiation, five Sikhs stand in their place.

games.q: you're the Guru. five men from different castes and regions have answered your call. how do you present them?
o: dressed alike, side by side, as one.
send each home to lead his own region.
games.why: tradition says they came out dressed alike beside the Guru: five beloved, from everywhere, as one.

practice: On each breath out, say one name, softly or in your head, and let its meaning come with it: Daya, compassion; Dharam, doing what's right; Himmat, courage; Mohkam, steadfastness; Sahib, dignity.
Then go around again, slower, and rest on the one you need most today.

wordCard.voice: Panj Pyare. The five beloved, the five who answered the Guru's call in 1699, from different castes and regions of India.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: panj, five; pyare, beloved ones.

carryVoice: Your line: daya, dharam, himmat, mohkam, sahib. Five names that, together, make one portrait. Eighty-five days now.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on the Panj Pyare, Anandpur, Vaisakhi 1699
